props.title: Hammett
props.initialSlug: Noir writer hunts missing girl in 1920s Chinatown

sections.content: Wim Wenders' neo-noir Hammett (1982) reimagines detective fiction pioneer Dashiell Hammett as the protagonist of exactly the kind of hardboiled mystery he would write. Frederic Forrest plays Hammett during his San Francisco years, when the former Pinkerton detective turned writer gets pulled into investigating the disappearance of a Chinese prostitute. The film merges fact and fiction, placing the real-life author of The Maltese Falcon (1941) into a stylized world that mirrors his own literary creations. Executive producer Francis Ford Coppola had Wenders reshoot significant portions, resulting in a fascinating hybrid of European art film sensibilities and classic Hollywood noir aesthetics.

sections.content: Hammett exists in fascinating dialogue with other films about writers and the blurring of art and life. Like Barton Fink (1991) and Adaptation (2002), it explores the mysterious alchemy between real experience and creative imagination. The film's production history - with Wenders' original vision being substantially altered by studio intervention - eerily parallels Hammett's own experience of seeing his literary work transformed by Hollywood. The resulting film maintains a dreamy uncertainty about what's "real" and what's "fiction" that suits its subject matter perfectly.

The film's visual style draws heavily from both German Expressionism and American film noir, appropriate for a story about the writer who helped bridge those traditions. Wenders and cinematographer Philip Lathrop create a shadowy 1920s San Francisco that feels both historically detailed and deliberately artificial, much like the world of Chinatown (1974) or The Two Jakes (1990). The movie's look influenced later neo-noirs like Miller's Crossing (1990) and L.A. Confidential (1997). SUBHEAD: Literary Detective Cinema

sections.content: Hammett belongs to a specific subset of noir films focused on writers of detective fiction, including The Long Goodbye (1973), which reimagined Raymond Chandler's Philip Marlowe in contemporary Los Angeles, and Poodle Springs (1998), which did the same for an aging Marlowe. These films comment on the genre while working within it, much as Hammett's own writing both defined and transcended pulp conventions. The movie's meta-textual elements anticipate later works like Wonder Boys (2000) and The Number 23 (2007) that explore the sometimes dangerous intersection of writing and reality.
